s06b.slug: FRIDAY · 10:25 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE KITCHEN SINK
body: The punch cups are Mrs. Fitch’s, cut glass to match the bowl, forty of them, and they don’t go in any machine. Father Osei has them in the sink in water as hot as the tap will give, his sleeves rolled to the elbow, the wooden rosary on his belt knocking the cabinet door every time he reaches for the bottom. The mistletoe lies on the drainboard beside the Lava where he set it down, tape and all. The dish towel has been over Jack’s shoulder since half past eight. Osei hands a wet cup back to him without turning around, and the towel has a job.

Through the doorway Julian has gone from the carols into something slower that Jack doesn’t know, and Lena’s alto is under it, keeping it company. Jack stands with his back to the doorway and dries. When the alto drops out for a bar, his hands stop on the cup until it comes back.
Osei talks, and none of it is about Jack. It’s about waiting rooms.

“At the hospital in Kumasi the waiting room was the most honest room in the building,” he says, rinsing. “Wooden benches. A fan in the ceiling that went round when there was power. Mothers with babies, old men with their sons, a farmer who had walked since morning with his hand wrapped in a shirt. Once a goat, which belonged to somebody and was also unwell.” Another cup comes back over his shoulder. “Nobody in it was pretending to be anywhere else. Upstairs on the wards everybody pretended — the patients that they felt better, the doctors that they knew. Downstairs people only waited, and told each other what for.”
He holds a cup up to the light over the stove, finds a print on it, and puts it back in the water.
“Advent is a waiting room with candles.”

His eyes go to Jack’s hands on the towel, to the black still under the nails. “Lemon,” he says. “For the battery. Lava will not reach it. Mrs. Fitch keeps a bag of lemons in the bottom of the refrigerator for the lemon bars.” He considers the refrigerator, and the punch bowl on top of it. “Do not tell her who told you.”

On the sill over the sink, propped against the glass behind the dish soap, there’s an airmail envelope with the red-and-blue border, stamped, addressed in a small upright hand. The last line says LONDON. Osei sees him see it.
“I post one every month,” he says. “December’s is late.” And he goes back into the water for the next cup.

Over the stove hangs a clock shaped like a teapot that somebody gave Newman House in a better decade. Twenty-five past ten. Jack looks at it, and when he looks away from it Osei’s eyes are just leaving it too, and going back to the cups.

response: “I’ve got somewhere to be.”
Osei rinses a cup and turns it in the light. “In Kumasi, a guest who leaves before the singing is finished is either in love or in debt.”
“Which am I?”
“I was a doctor.” He hands the cup across. “I don’t diagnose at parties.”

He pulls the plug, and the sink starts down with a long complaint in the pipes. “Saturday I am in the closet at half past three,” he says, drying his own hands on his trousers, since Jack has the towel. “And my door is the one with the light on. I sleep badly. It may as well be useful.”
He holds out his hand for the towel. Jack gives it to him, and Osei folds it once over the oven handle and squares it there. “Ɛyɛ,” he says, and goes back out to his party.

response: “Does the mistletoe go in the drawer with the spray tan?”

Osei considers the sprig on the drainboard and moves it away from the clean cups with the back of a wet wrist. “With the spray tan, a flask from 2007, and a collar that belonged to a ferret.” He goes back to the water. “It is a very ecumenical drawer.”

“Pray for me, Father.”
“I do,” Osei says, surprised to be asked. “It is cheaper than worrying, and it works on Tuesdays.” He hands back the last cup. “And on Fridays, if you are not fussy.”

s10a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: He knocks — gently; the card is very clear — and goes in.

The coat closet hasn’t changed in a week. The kneeler on this side, the folding chair on the other, the linen screen in the middle on its wooden frame with the purple of a stole showing through; the coat hooks from 1962 along the back wall; the Prodigal Son thumbtacked inside the door at the height of a kneeling man’s eyes. On the far side the chair takes the priest’s weight, and the bad leg gets itself arranged, and after that there’s nothing to hear but Mrs. Fitch’s pencil out at the card table, and that only because he’s listening for it.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.”
“It’s been a week since my last confession.”
He had it in order out there. In here it comes the way it wants to.

“You told me to change the hour,” he says. “To keep her in the daylight. I did, once. Thursday afternoon. The harbor, a man hosing down a boat, her sitting on the back of her car with a sleeve of pencils. It was easy.” There’s still black in the creases of his knuckles from a battery in Buellton, and he looks at that. “Then it got dark.”
Osei waits.

“Thursday night I went to her house. Her room. I knew what I was going there for.” He keeps his voice down, though there’s no need. “And I said no. And it stopped. Every other time it was something else that stopped it — her phone, a fire alarm, somebody knocking on a door. Thursday it was me.”

“She didn’t understand it, at first. She was afraid I thought less of her. Because of what she’d wanted.” He has the words she used and leaves them where they are. “So I told her I didn’t. And then she asked me why I’d said no, and I told her that too, and then she asked me everything. Till four in the morning. What a mortal sin is. Whether the nuns told the boys the same thing. What I say to you in here.” Something close to a laugh gets out of him. “She wanted every answer. She kept them all.”
“And she heard you?”
“She heard all of it. She argued with half of it. Then she went and made tea and came back with more questions.”
“On her porch I asked her for daylight. She said Sunday. She’s going to teach me to surf.”
“And I told her —” This is the one. “I told her I’m not saying it’s always going to be no. Not until — I didn’t promise her that. I said it’s a no right now. She said she could work with that.”

“Last night she argued me out of it. Nearly.” He makes himself say the rest in order. “She took the sentence apart. The whole thing, point by point. She was funny, and she was right about half of it, and then she asked me if it was still right now. I said it was. I said no again.”
“And she stopped there. Only there. Whatever we’d been doing before she started, she went back to, and kept on with it, all night.”

body.text: “And I didn’t hold any of the rest back. I didn’t want to.”

body: The rest of the week comes after that, a piece at a time.
“Monday there was a trailer door. She was leaving, and I caught her wrist.”
“She sent me a picture. I kept it. And what I said back.”

body.text: “I’ve lied to people about where I go.”
“I lied to her, too. Something small, about who ended up with a present.”
“And the rest of the week,” he says, and that’s as far as it goes. Osei lets it stand.

body: “I keep putting myself in the near occasion,” Jack says, in the old words, because they are still the right ones.
Osei is quiet. When he speaks it’s the doctor first, with the dull question.
“Thursday night,” he says. “Did you go to her, or did she come for you?”
“I called her.”
“Why that night?”
“I heard a song.”
“Whose song?”
“Somebody else’s.”

And then, because it isn’t the whole of the answer and he’s in the one room where he can’t leave it there: “But that isn’t why I go.” It comes out faster than he meant. “It made it that night. It isn’t why. I’d have gone anyway. I go because I want to be there, Father. I like her. I like being with her.” He has run out of the right words and goes on with the ones he’s got. “She wants to know how everything works. Why I think what I think — she takes it apart and puts it back and hands it to me. She makes me laugh till it hurts. She’s good at things I’ve never tried and she makes me try them. I want to know all of her. That’s the truth. She isn’t somewhere I go to feel better.”
On the other side of the screen the priest is quiet for a while. When he speaks, the doctor has stepped out of the room.
“I believe you,” Osei says. “I have heard a great many young men describe a girl in here, my friend. Some of them describe a medicine. Some of them describe an alibi. You have described a person.”

“You told me she was frightened of what you thought of her, and you told her the truth. You told me she was curious — that she wanted every answer, and argued with half of them, and kept them all. You told me you stopped it yourself, with no telephone and no alarm, and then you stayed.” Something comes out of him that is nearly a laugh, and a kind one. “And then she offered you daylight. I prescribe daylight, and the patient books an appointment at dawn, in December, in the sea. Go. Fall off the board. Fall off it many times. It is a very good hour to be bad at something.”

“Saint Thomas says that to love is to will the good of the other. Not to want her — you want her; you have told me so, and I believe that too. To *will her good*. Everything you have said to me this afternoon is a young man willing a girl’s good, and delighting in her while he does it. That is real. It is good, and it comes from God, and I want you to hear me say so before I say anything else.”
A breath, on the far side of the linen.

“And that is exactly why it is dangerous. Nobody is tempted by a thing that is only bad. A man does not risk his soul over a girl he doesn’t care for. The occasion is near because what is in it is good — and the better it is, the nearer it comes.”

“Now.” The doctor again, gently. “The door. Telling her the truth about yourself was not a sin. You were honest about your weakness, and that is rarer than you think. But hear what you have done. A no that is only for tonight has to be said again tomorrow night. In medicine we would call that a dose, not a cure — it wears off by morning. You have signed up to say it every night, to a woman who heard you the first time and argued the second.”
He waits until Jack has heard all of it.
“Can you?”

choices.key: Father Osei asked if you can say no every night to a woman who heard you the first time. You said you’ll say it every night.
response: “Then I’ll say it every night,” Jack says.
“Then say it before you get in the car,” Osei says. “Not after. Before is a decision. After is a negotiation, and nobody has ever won a negotiation at two in the morning.”

“For your penance, a decade for her. By her name,” Osei says. “And with every one, ask God for her good — the thing you already want for her. Ask it plainly, so you hear what it is.” A pause. “And one Hail Mary for whoever wrote the song.”
Jack says the Act of Contrition. He has been saying it since he was seven. Today it catches on *firmly resolve*, and he goes back for the words and says them again, slower.
Osei’s hand comes up.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“The Lord has freed you from your sins. Go in peace.”

While he was in there the blue panes have climbed off the pews and gone up the far wall, thinner. He kneels in the back pew under what’s left of them and breathes to the bottom of his lungs, for the first time since Thursday.
He prays the decade on his knuckles, ten times round, with her name at the front of every one. *Skye.* The extra one he says for Julian, by name, because the priest didn’t have it to give him.

Up at the votive rack under the Marian shrine Lena is still on her knees, and there’s one more candle burning than when he went in. She doesn’t turn around. He doesn’t go over. The picture is still in his jacket, unopened.

s10o.slug: SATURDAY · 4:55 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, FR. OSEI’S OFFICE
body: The office is the one Jack remembers from September: the stethoscope on its hook by the window, the chessboard on the side table with a game still standing on it and the white bishop with the chip out of its shoulder, and highlife on the record player, guitars and a horn line going round like a wheel. Osei lifts the needle off in the middle of the song, and the room goes quiet enough to hear the courtyard.

He lays the pipe wrench across the desk blotter and doesn’t bother with the rubber boots. Out of his cardigan pocket he takes a purple stole, kisses it, and puts it on over the cardigan. He pulls the second chair out from the wall and sets it beside his own, both of them facing the crucifix on the far wall instead of each other.
“Face to face is permitted,” he says, lowering himself into the one on the left, the bad leg last. “Side by side is easier on everybody.”

Past the window the families are going in to the five o’clock in their coats. “They will start without me,” Osei says. “Mrs. Fitch will give them a rosary. They like it when I am late. It makes them feel holy.”
Jack sits down beside him. The crucifix has them both.

“Go and rejoice,” he says. “It is tomorrow’s homily. You have had a preview.”

He goes ahead across the courtyard in his rubber boots, toward the sacristy, at the speed the leg allows. Through the open doors of the church Mrs. Fitch has the five o’clock on the third Joyful Mystery and is not waiting for anybody.

Jack sits on the wall under the olive tree and prays the decade on his knuckles, ten times round, with her name at the front of every one. *Skye.* The extra one he says for Julian, by name, because the priest didn’t have it to give him. Inside, the rosary stops in the middle of a word, and the organ comes in over it. The picture is still in his jacket, unopened.

s10b.slug: SATURDAY · 4:45 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD
body: He got up off the folding chair at ten to four, when it was his turn, and Mrs. Fitch said it to her crossword as he went past the card table: “Father keeps a chair warm for the ones who come back, Mr. Costigan.”

He didn’t go far. The low wall under the olive tree is fifty feet from the side door, and he has been on it most of an hour with the RAZR shut in his hand. The outer screen has its envelope. He hasn’t opened it. The wind came around cold off the water at noon and hasn’t let up; it goes through the olive tree in gusts and turns the leaves silver side up, and the sun is down on the roofs of Las Olas, gold, nearly gone. Across Ocean Road the windows of Delgado have started coming on, one floor at a time.
At twenty past four Lena came out the side door in her coat, done with her prayers, and saw him on the wall. She lifted a hand. He lifted his. She went on down the path to Ocean Road.

Now the five o’clock is coming across the courtyard: a man carrying a girl asleep on his shoulder, two grandmothers arm in arm against the wind, a boy in a clip-on tie being steered by the collar. Inside, the closet door will be standing open on nobody.

Father Osei comes out of Newman House in rubber boots, with a pipe wrench the length of his forearm. He has a quarter of an hour before his own Mass and he means to spend it on the sprinkler: the brass head standing up dead out of its crust of dried mud by the wall, shut off at the valve since November. He sees Jack, and comes over to the wall as though they’d arranged it.
“Mrs. Fitch tells me I was one short this afternoon,” he says. “She counts. It is her charism.”
He gets down — slowly; the leg — beside the valve box set in the dirt at the foot of the wall, and holds the wrench out to Jack. “Hold this.”

Jack holds it. Osei lifts the iron lid off the box and clears a winter of olive leaves out of it with his bare hand, and a snail, which he sets on top of the wall. They fit the jaws to the valve together, and Jack leans on the handle, and Osei puts his own hands over Jack’s and leans too. The valve doesn’t move. They try it the other way, in case. It doesn’t move that way either. The sprinkler head stands up out of the mud as it has since November.
“Brass, 1962,” Osei says. “Installed by an optimist. I try it every Saturday after the line. It is good for my humility, and for nothing else.”
Osei sits down on the wall beside him to rest the leg, and breathes, and considers the sprinkler. The snail has started down the far side of the wall.
“The closet closes at a quarter to five,” he says. “My office doesn’t. I told you where the light is.”

response: “Now?”

“Now is the only time I have ever been any good at.” He takes the wrench back and gets up off the wall, and goes ahead of Jack across the courtyard toward Newman House, slowly, the bad leg setting the pace, against the families going the other way into church.

choices.key: Father Osei came out with a pipe wrench and offered you his office. You told him not today.
response: “Not today, Father.”
“Then I will see you at nine tomorrow,” Osei says, “and the light will still be on. It is on a timer. I am cheap.”
He gets up, and gives the valve one more try on his own, for luck, and it doesn’t give for him either. He goes in with the wrench under his arm to say his Mass.

body: At nine on Gaudete Sunday the hull of St. Brendan’s holds candlelight up to the ribs, and the blue glass is black and full of the church’s own reflection. In the vestibule Joey Abruzzo has stopped Father Osei on his way to the procession to point at the vestments. They come out once a year: old silk gone soft, rose, smelling faintly of the cupboard.
“It is not pink,” Osei says.
“Father, it’s a little —”
“It is *rose*, Joseph. Go and sit down.”

Lena and Julian have the pew in front, Lena in the mantilla with her missal, Julian with the hymnal already open and held low where she can read it. Jack takes the end of the next pew beside Kevin, where he usually is.

body.text: Kevin moves his coat over for him. “Thirteen and oh,” he says, low. “You’d have liked it.”

body: Gus brings the organ in, and the choir comes up the aisle behind the cross singing in Latin — *Gaudete, gaudete* — Gus’s own arrangement, all voices welcome and every one of them taking him up on it: Kenzie on top, Mrs. Fitch’s descant over Kenzie, Joey flat and proud at the back of the line. Beside Jack, Kevin sings the bass from the pew, steady and true, now that the whole Newman Center knows he can. At the wreath Kenzie peels off with a taper and lights the third candle, the rose one, beside the two violet, and the front pews sit back to look at it. In the pew in front Lena watches the new flame take, with her missal shut on one finger, until it stands up straight.

Zephaniah. The psalm, with Kenzie’s capo halfway up the neck. Paul to the Philippians: *Rejoice in the Lord always. I shall say it again: rejoice.* And then Luke, and John at the river, and the crowds coming down to him with a question.
Osei comes down out of the chair and stands at the head of the aisle in the rose vestments, with the bad leg resting.

“Three times in this Gospel people come to John with the same question,” he says. “The crowds. The tax collectors. The soldiers. *What then should we do?* And notice what John does not tell them. He does not say, leave your lives and come and eat locusts with me in the desert. He has eaten the locusts. He does not recommend them.” The church laughs, the low laugh of a full church at nine at night. “He says: you with two coats, give one away. You who collect the taxes, stop taking more than you are owed. You soldiers, be content with your pay. The next honest thing, in the life you already have.”

“And Zephaniah, who is not a cheerful man, says the strangest sentence in his book. *The Lord, your God, is in your midst. He will rejoice over you with gladness. He will sing joyfully because of you.*” He lets the church hold it. “God, singing. Over you. Over the soldier and the tax collector, and over the man who is still making up his mind about the coat.”

“Saint Paul says rejoice, and in case you were not listening, he says it again. Rejoice is a command, which means it isn’t a feeling. You can obey it on a bad week.” He looks out at the pews, at the backpacks under them and the finals in everybody’s faces. “Many of you are having a bad week. The candle is lit anyway.”
He goes back up to the chair, and the church sits in the quiet after it. Jack sits in it with his hands between his knees until the Creed stands him up.
At the sign of peace Lena turns around in the pew in front. “Peace, Youngstown.” And her hand. Julian turns with her and shakes Kevin’s hand, and then Jack’s, warmly, the way he shakes everybody’s.

After Communion the choir gives them *Gaudete* again, softer, and on the last high note Mrs. Fitch’s descant cracks clean in half, and she finishes it anyway, louder, and Gus at the organ bows his head over the keys to keep his face to himself.

After the last hymn the church empties out toward the doors and the cold. Father Osei is on the top step in the rose vestments with the leg resting against the rail, shaking hands with everybody who comes past him. When it’s Jack’s turn he takes the hand in both of his.

body.else: “Mr. Costigan. The light is still on.”

body: Mrs. Fitch arrives at his elbow about candle wax on the carpet, and Osei lets go of Jack to hear about it.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday I held the wrench for him at the courtyard wall. The sprinkler won. Gaudete: rejoice is a command.
